Global well-posedness for Euler-Boussinesq system with critical dissipation

Abstract.

In this paper we study a fractional diffusion Boussinesq model which couples the incompressible Euler equation for the velocity and a transport equation with fractional diffusion for the temperature. We prove global well-posedness results.

Key words and phrases: 
Boussinesq system, transport equations, paradifferential calculus
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
76D03 (35B33 35Q35 76D05)

1. Introduction

Boussinesq systems of the type

{∂tv+v⋅∇v+∇p=θ​e2+ν​𝒟v​v∂tθ+v⋅∇θ=κ​𝒟θ​θdiv​v=0v|t=0=v0,θ|t=0=θ0\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v+\nabla p=\theta e_{2}+\nu\mathcal{D}_{v}v\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta=\kappa\mathcal{D}_{\theta}\theta\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ v_{|t=0}=v^{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta^{0}\end{array}\right.

are simple models widely used in the modelling of oceanic and atmospheric motions. These models also appear in many other physical problems, we refer for instance to [5, 3] for more details. Here, we focus on the two-dimensional case, the space variable x=(x1,x2)x=(x_{1},x_{2}) is in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, the velocity field vv is given by v=(v1,v2)v=(v^{1},v^{2}) and the pressure pp and the temperature θ\theta are scalar functions. The factor θ​e2\theta e_{2} in the velocity equation, the vector e2e_{2} being given by (0,1)(0,1), models the effect of gravity on the fluid motion. The operator 𝒟v\mathcal{D}_{v} and 𝒟θ\mathcal{D}_{\theta} whose form may vary are used to take into account the possible effects of diffusion and dissipation in the fluid motion, thus the constants ν≥0\nu\geq 0, κ≥0\kappa\geq 0 can be seen as the inverse of Reynolds numbers.

Mathematically, the simplest model to study is the fully viscous model when ν>0\nu>0, κ>0\kappa>0 and 𝒟v=Δ\mathcal{D}_{v}=\Delta, 𝒟θ=Δ.\mathcal{D}_{\theta}=\Delta. The properties of the system are very similar to the one of the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equation and similar global well-posedness results can be obtained.

The most difficult model for the mathematical study is the inviscid one, i.e. when ν=κ=0\nu=\kappa=0. A local existence result of smooth solution can be proven as for symmetric hyperbolic quasilinear systems, nevertheless, it is not known if smooth solutions can develop singularities in finite time. Indeed, the temperature θ\theta is the solution of a transport equation and the vorticity ω=curl ​v=∂1v2−∂2v1\omega=\mbox{curl }v=\partial_{1}v^{2}-\partial_{2}v^{1} solves the equation

(1.1) ∂tω+v⋅∇ω=∂1θ.\partial_{t}\omega+v\cdot\nabla\omega=\partial_{1}\theta.

The main difficulty is that to get an L∞L^{\infty} estimate on ω\omega which is crucial to prove global existence of smooth solutions for Euler type equation, one needs to estimate ∫0T‖∂1θ‖L∞\int_{0}^{T}||\partial_{1}\theta||_{L^{\infty}} and, unfortunately, no a priori estimate on ∂1θ\partial_{1}\theta is known.

In order to understand the coupling between the two equations in Boussinesq type systems, there have been many recent works studying Boussinesq systems with partial viscosity i.e. with a viscous term only in one equation. For κ>0\kappa>0, ν=0\nu=0 and 𝒟θ=Δ\mathcal{D}_{\theta}=\Delta, the question of global existence is solved recently in a series of papers. In [7], Chae proved the global existence and uniqueness for initial data (v0,θ0)∈Hs×Hs,(v^{0},\theta^{0})\in H^{s}\times H^{s}, with s>2,s>2, see also [20]. This result was recently extended in [16] by the two first authors to initial data v0∈Bp,12p+1v^{0}\in B_{p,1}^{\frac{2}{p}+1} and θ0∈Bp,1−1+2p∩Lr,r>2\theta^{0}\in B_{p,1}^{-1+\frac{2}{p}}\cap L^{r},r>2. More recently, the study of global existence of Yudovich solutions for this system has been done in [14]. We also mention that in [15], Danchin and Paicu were able to construct global strong solutions (still for κ>0\kappa>0, ν=0\nu=0) for a dissipative term of the form 𝒟θ=∂11θ\mathcal{D}_{\theta}=\partial_{11}\theta instead of Δ​θ.\Delta\theta. Recently the first author and Zerguine [19] proved the global well-posedness for fractional diffusion 𝒟θ=−|D|α\mathcal{D}_{\theta}=-|\textnormal{D}|^{\alpha} for α∈]1,2[\alpha\in]1,2[ where the operator |D|α|\textnormal{D}|^{\alpha} is defined by

ℱ⁡(|D|α​u)​(ξ)=|ξ|α​(ℱ​u)​(ξ).\mathcal{F}(|\textnormal{D}|^{\alpha}u)(\xi)=|\xi|^{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}u)(\xi).

In these works, the global existence result relies on the fact that the only smoothing effect due to the transport-(fractional) diffusion equation

∂tθ+v⋅∇θ+|D|α​θ=0\partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta+|\textnormal{D}|^{\alpha}\theta=0

governing the temperature is sufficient to counterbalance the amplification of the vorticity. However the case α=1\alpha=1 is not reached by their method. The main reason is that this case can be seen as critical in the previous approaches in the sense that the smoothing effect for the temperature equation does not provide the LT1​(L∞)L^{1}_{T}(L^{\infty}) bound for ∂1θ\partial_{1}\theta which seems needed to control the amplification of the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the vorticity. Note that such an estimate is nevertheless almost true since ∂1θ\partial_{1}\theta can be estimated in the space L~T1​(L∞)\tilde{L}^{1}_{T}(L^{\infty}) which has the same scaling (see below for the definition). The aim of this paper is the study of the well-posedness for this case, i.e., we focus on the system

(1.2) {∂tv+v⋅∇v+∇p=θ​e2∂tθ+v⋅∇θ+|D|​θ=0div​v=0v|t=0=v0,θ|t=0=θ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v+\nabla p=\theta e_{2}\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta+|\textnormal{D}|\theta=0\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ v_{|t=0}=v^{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta^{0}.\end{array}\right.

Note that we have taken κ=1\kappa=1 which is legitimate since we study global well-posedness issues. Indeed, we can always change the coefficient κ\kappa into 11 by a change of scale.

We also point out that at first sight, the system (1.2) contains the mathematical difficulties of the critical quasigeostrophic equation introduced in [10]

(1.3) ∂tθ+v⋅∇θ+|D|​θ=0,v=∇⟂|D|−1​θ\partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta+|\textnormal{D}|\theta=0,\quad v=\nabla^{\perp}|\textnormal{D}|^{-1}\theta

which was much studied recently. Indeed, in (1.2) the link between vv and θ\theta is not given by the Riesz transform but by a dynamical equation, the first equation of (1.2). Nevertheless, from this velocity equation one gets that vv has basically the regularity of θ\theta as in the quasigeostrophic equation. The global well-posedness for (1.3) was obtained recently by Kiselev, Nasarov and Volberg [21]. We also refer to the work [6] by Caffarelli and Vasseur about the regularity of weak solutions. Other discussions can be found in [1, 11, 12].

The main result of this paper is a global well-posedness result for the system (1.2) (see section 2 for the definitions and the basic properties of Besov spaces).

Theorem 1.1.

Let p∈]2,∞[p\in]2,\infty[, v0∈B∞,11∩W˙1,pv^{0}\in{B}_{\infty,1}^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,p} be a divergence-free vector field of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and θ0∈B∞,10∩Lp\theta^{0}\in B_{\infty,1}^{0}\cap L^{p}. Then there exists a unique global solution (v,θ)(v,\theta) to the system (1.2) with

v∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,B∞,11∩W˙1,p),θ∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,B∞,10∩Lp)∩L~loc1​(ℝ+,Bp,∞1).v\in L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}\big(\mathbb{R}_{+};{B}_{\infty,1}^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,p}),\qquad\theta\in L_{\textnormal{loc}}^{\infty}\big(\mathbb{R}_{+};B_{\infty,1}^{0}\cap L^{p}\big)\cap\widetilde{L}_{\textnormal{loc}}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};{B}_{p,\infty}^{1}).

A few remarks are in order.

Remark 1.2.

If we take θ=0\theta=0 then the system (1.2) is reduced to the well-known 2D incompressible Euler system. It is well known that this system is globally well-posed in HsH^{s} for s>2s>2. The main argument for globalization is the BKM criterion [2] ensuring that the development of finite time singularities for Kato’s solutions is related to the blowup of the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the vorticity near the maximal time existence. In [26] Vishik has extended the global existence of strong solutions result to initial data lying on the spaces Bp,11+2/p.B_{p,1}^{1+2/p}. Notice that these spaces have the same scaling as Lipschitz functions (the space which is relevant for the hyperbolic theory) and in this sense they are called critical. We emphasize that the application of the BKM criterion requires a super-lipschitzian regularity (HsH^{s} with s>2s>2 for example). For that reason the question of global existence in the critical spaces Bp,11+2/pB_{p,1}^{1+2/p} is hard to deal with because these spaces have only a lipschitzian regularity and the BKM criterion cannot be used.

Since Bp,11+2/p↪B∞,11∩W˙1,rB_{p,1}^{1+2/p}\hookrightarrow{B}_{\infty,1}^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,r} for all p∈[1,+∞[p\in[1,+\infty[ and r>max⁡{p,2}r>\max\{p,2\}, then the space of initial velocity in our theorem contains all the critical spaces Bp,11+2/pB_{p,1}^{1+2/p} except the biggest one, that is B∞,11B_{\infty,1}^{1}. For the limiting case we have been able to prove the global existence only up to the extra assumption ∇v0∈Lp\nabla v^{0}\in L^{p} for some p∈]2,∞[p\in]2,\infty[. The reason behind this extra assumption is the fact that to obtain a global L∞L^{\infty} bound for the vorticity we need before to establish an LpL^{p} estimate for some p∈]2,∞[p\in]2,\infty[ and it is not clear how to get rid of this condition.

Remark 1.3.

Since ∇v,∇θ∈Lloc1​(ℝ+,L∞)\nabla v,\nabla\theta\in L^{1}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\infty}) (see Remark 5.6 below for θ\theta) then we can easily propagate all the higher regularities: critical (i.e. v0∈Bp,11+2/pv_{0}\in B_{p,1}^{1+2/p} with pp finite) and sub-critical (for example v0∈Hsv_{0}\in H^{s}, for s>2s>2).

The main idea in the proof of Theorem 1.1 is to really used the structural properties of the system solved by (ω,θ)(\omega,\theta), ω=curl ​v=∂1v2−∂2v1\omega=\mbox{curl }v=\partial_{1}v^{2}-\partial_{2}v^{1}. Indeed, if we neglect the nonlinear terms for the moment, one gets the system

∂tω=∂1θ,∂tθ=−|D|​θ\partial_{t}\omega=\partial_{1}\theta,\quad\partial_{t}\theta=-|\textnormal{D}|\theta

and we notice that its symbol given by

𝒜⁡(ξ)=(0i​ξ10−|ξ|)\mathcal{A}(\xi)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&i\xi_{1}\\ 0&-|\xi|\end{array}\right)

is diagonalizable for ξ≠0\xi\neq 0 with two real distinct eigenvalues which are 00 and −|ξ|-|\xi|. By using the Riesz transform ℛ=∂1/|D|\mathcal{R}={\partial_{1}/|\textnormal{D}|}, one gets that the diagonal form of the system is given by

∂tℛ​θ=|D|​ℛ​θ,∂t(ω+ℛ​θ)=0.\partial_{t}\mathcal{R}\theta=|\textnormal{D}|\mathcal{R}\theta,\quad\partial_{t}\big(\omega+\mathcal{R}\theta\big)=0.

This last form of the system is much more convenient in order to perform a priori estimates. To prove Theorem 1.1, we shall use the same idea, we shall diagonalize the linear part of the system and then get a priori estimates from the study of the new system. The main technical difficulty in this program when one takes the nonlinear terms into account is to evaluate in a sufficiently sharp way the commutator [ℛ,v⋅∇][\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla] between the Riesz transform and the convection operator. Such commutator estimates are stated and proven in section 3 of the paper.

The diagonalization approach used in this paper also allows to prove global well-posedness in different spaces for a ”Boussinesq-Navier-Stokes” system i.e. the system which corresponds to 𝒟θ=0\mathcal{D}_{\theta}=0 and 𝒟v=−|D|\mathcal{D}_{v}=-|\textnormal{D}|. This is discussed in a companion paper [18].

The remaining of the paper is organized as follows. In section 2 we recall some functional spaces and we give some of their useful properties. Section 3 is devoted to the study of some commutators involving the Riesz transform. In section 4 we study a linear transport-(fractional) diffusion equation. Especially, we establish some smoothing effects and a logarithmic estimate type.

In section 5 we give the proof of Theorem 1.1 which is It is splitted into three parts. We first establish some a priori estimates, then we prove the uniqueness and finally we briefly explain how one can easily combine a procedure of smoothing out of the initial data with the a priori estimates to get the existence part of the theorem. An appendix is devoted to the proof of a technical commutator lemma.

In the next proposition we gather some properties of the Riez operator ℛ=∂1/|D|.\mathcal{R}={\partial_{1}}/{|D|}.

Proposition 3.1.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the Riez operator ℛ=∂1/|D|.\mathcal{R}={\partial_{1}}/{|D|}. Then the following hold true.

  1. (1)

    For every p∈]1,+∞[,p\in]1,+\infty[,

    ‖ℛ‖ℒ⁡(Lp)≲1.\|\mathcal{R}\|_{\mathcal{L}(L^{p})}\lesssim 1.
  2. (2)

    Let χ∈𝒟⁡(ℝd)\chi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Then, there exists C>0C>0 such that

    ‖|D|s​χ​(2−q​|D|)​ℛ‖ℒ⁡(Lp)≤C​2q​s,\||\textnormal{D}|^{s}\chi(2^{-q}|\textnormal{D}|)\mathcal{R}\|_{\mathcal{L}(L^{p})}\leq C2^{qs},

    We notice that the previous results hold true if we change |D|s|\textnormal{D}|^{s} by ∇s\nabla^{s} with s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N}.

    Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a fixed ring. Then, there exists ψ∈𝒮\psi\in\mathcal{S} whose spectum does not meet the origin such that

Proof.

(1) It is a classical Calderón-Zygmund theorem (see [24] for instance).

(2) Let K∈𝒮′K\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime} such that ℱ​K​(ξ)=|ξ|s​χ​(|ξ|)​ξi|ξ|.\mathcal{F}K(\xi)=|\xi|^{s}\chi(|\xi|)\frac{\xi_{i}}{|\xi|}. KK is a tempered distribution such that its Fourier transform ℱ​K\mathcal{F}K is 𝒞∞​(ℝd∖{0})\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\}) and satisfies for every α∈ℕd\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{d}

|∂ξαℱ​K​(ξ)|≤Cα​|ξ|s−|α|.|\partial_{\xi}^{\alpha}\mathcal{F}K(\xi)|\leq C_{\alpha}|\xi|^{s-|\alpha|}.

According to Mikhlin-Hörmander Theorem (see [24] for instance) we have for every α∈ℕd\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{d} and x∈ℝd∖{0}x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\},

|∂xαK⁡(x)|≤Cα′​|x|−s−d−|α|.|\partial_{x}^{\alpha}K(x)|\leq C_{\alpha}^{\prime}|x|^{-s-d-|\alpha|}.

Then, it ensues that

|K⁡(x)|≤C​|x|−d−s∀x≠0.|K(x)|\leq C|x|^{-d-s}\qquad\forall x\neq 0.

Since ℱ​K\mathcal{F}K is obviously in L1L^{1}, we also have that K∈𝒞0​(ℝd)K\in\mathcal{C}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). This removes the singularity at the origin and gives

|K⁡(x)|≤C​(1+|x|)−d−s∀x∈ℝd.|K(x)|\leq C(1+|x|)^{-d-s}\qquad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Therefore we get that the kernel K∈L1K\in L^{1}. Now for every u∈Lpu\in L^{p} we have |D|s​ℛ​χ​(|D|)​u=K⋆u.|\textnormal{D}|^{s}\mathcal{R}\chi(|\textnormal{D}|)u=K\star u. We can now conclude the case q=0q=0 by using the classical Young inequality for convolution products.
The case q≥1q\geq 1 can be derived from q=0q=0 via an obvious argument of homogeneity.

The following lemma will be useful in the proof of many commutator estimates.

Lemma 3.2.

Given (p,m)∈[1,∞]2(p,m)\in[1,\infty]^{2} such that p≥m′p\geq m^{\prime} with m′m^{\prime} the conjugate exponent of mm. Let f,gf,g and hh be three functions such that ∇f∈Lp,g∈Lm\nabla f\in L^{p},g\in L^{m} and x​h∈Lm′xh\in L^{m^{\prime}}. Then,

‖h⋆(f​g)−f⁡(h⋆g)‖Lp≤‖x​h‖Lm′​‖∇f‖Lp​‖g‖Lm.\|h\star(fg)-f(h\star g)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|xh\|_{L^{m^{\prime}}}\|\nabla f\|_{L^{p}}\|g\|_{L^{m}}.
Proof.

We have by definition and Taylor formula

h⋆(f​g)​(x)−f⁡(h⋆g)​(x)\displaystyle h\star(fg)(x)-f(h\star g)(x) =\displaystyle= ∫ℝdh⁡(x−y)​g​(y)​(f⁡(y)−f⁡(x))​𝑑y\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}h(x-y)g(y)\big(f(y)-f(x)\big)dy
=\displaystyle= ∫01∫ℝdg⁡(y)​h​(x−y)​[(y−x)⋅∇f​(x+t⁡(y−x))]​𝑑y​𝑑t.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}g(y)h(x-y)\Big[(y-x)\cdot\nabla f(x+t(y-x))\Big]dydt.

Using Hölder inequalities and making a change of variables z=t⁡(x−y)z=t(x-y) we get

|h⋆(f​g)​(x)−f⁡(h⋆g)​(x)|≤‖g‖Lm​∫01(∫ℝdt−d​h1m′​(t−1​z)​|∇f|m′​(x−z)​𝑑z)1m′,|h\star(fg)(x)-f(h\star g)(x)|\leq\|g\|_{L^{m}}\int_{0}^{1}\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}t^{-d}h_{1}^{m^{\prime}}(t^{-1}z)|\nabla f|^{m^{\prime}}(x-z)dz\Big)^{\frac{1}{m^{\prime}}},

where we set h1​(z)=|z|​|h⁡(z)|.h_{1}(z)=|z||h(z)|. Using Convolution inequalities we obtain since p≥m′p\geq m^{\prime}

‖h⋆(f​g)−f⁡(h⋆g)‖Lp\displaystyle\|h\star(fg)-f(h\star g)\|_{L^{p}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖g‖Lm​‖h1m′‖L11m′​‖|∇f|m′‖Lpm′1m′\displaystyle\|g\|_{L^{m}}\|h_{1}^{m^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}}^{\frac{1}{m^{\prime}}}\||\nabla f|^{m^{\prime}}\|_{L^{\frac{p}{m^{\prime}}}}^{\frac{1}{m^{\prime}}}
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖g‖Lm​‖h1‖Lm′​‖∇f‖Lp.\displaystyle\|g\|_{L^{m}}\|h_{1}\|_{L^{m^{\prime}}}\|\nabla f\|_{L^{p}}.

As explained in the introduction, the control of the commutator between ℛ\mathcal{R} and the convection operator v⋅∇v\cdot\nabla is a crucial ingredient in the proof of Theorem 1.1.

Theorem 3.3.

Let vv be is a smooth divergence-free vector field.

  1. (1)

    For every (p,r)∈[2,∞[×[1,∞](p,r)\in[2,\infty[\times[1,\infty] there exists a constant C=C⁡(p,r)C=C(p,r) such that

    ∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ∥Bp,r0≤C∥∇v∥Lp(∥θ∥B∞,r0+∥θ∥Lp),\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}}\leq C\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\big(\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,r}^{0}}+\|\theta\|_{L^{p}}\big),

    for every smooth scalar function θ\theta.

  2. (2)

    For every (r,ρ)∈[1,∞]×]1,∞[(r,\rho)\in[1,\infty]\times]1,\infty[ and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 there exists a constant C=C⁡(r,ρ,ε)C=C(r,\rho,\varepsilon) such that

    ∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ∥B∞,r0≤C(∥ω∥L∞+∥ω∥Lρ)(∥θ∥B∞,rϵ+∥θ∥Lρ),\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\|_{B_{\infty,r}^{0}}\leq C(\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\omega\|_{L^{\rho}})\big(\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,r}^{\epsilon}}+\|\theta\|_{L^{\rho}}\big),

    for every smooth scalar function θ\theta.

Proof.

We split the commutator into three parts, according to Bony’s decomposition,

[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ\displaystyle[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta =\displaystyle= ∑q∈ℕ[ℛ,Sq−1v⋅∇]Δqθ+∑q∈ℕ[ℛ,Δqv⋅∇]Sq−1θ\displaystyle\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}[\mathcal{R},S_{q-1}v\cdot\nabla]\Delta_{q}\theta+\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v\cdot\nabla]S_{q-1}\theta
+\displaystyle+ ∑q≥−1[ℛ,Δqv⋅∇]Δ~qθ\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq-1}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v\cdot\nabla]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta
=\displaystyle= ∑q∈ℕIq+∑q∈ℕIIq+∑q≥−1IIIq\displaystyle\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}\mbox{I}_{q}+\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}\mbox{II}_{q}+\sum_{q\geq-1}\mbox{III}_{q}
=\displaystyle= I+II+III.\displaystyle\mbox{I}+\mbox{II}+\mbox{III}.

We start with the estimate of the first term I. According to the point (3) of Proposition 3.1 there exists h∈𝒮h\in\mathcal{S} whose spectum does not meet the origin such that

Iq(x)=hq⋆(Sq−1v⋅∇Δqθ)−Sq−1v⋅(hq⋆∇Δqθ),\mbox{I}_{q}(x)=h_{q}\star(S_{q-1}v\cdot\nabla\Delta_{q}\theta)-S_{q-1}v\cdot(h_{q}\star\nabla\Delta_{q}\theta),

where hq​(x)=2d​q​h​(2q​x)h_{q}(x)=2^{dq}h(2^{q}x). Applying Lemma 3.2 with m=∞m=\infty we get

(3.1) ‖Iq‖Lp\displaystyle\|\mbox{I}_{q}\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∥xhq∥L1∥∇Sq−1v∥Lp∥Δq∇θ∥L∞\displaystyle\|xh_{q}\|_{L^{1}}\|\nabla S_{q-1}v\|_{L^{p}}\|\Delta_{q}\nabla\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖Δq​θ‖L∞.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}.

In the last line we’ve used Bernstein inequality and ‖x​hq‖L1=2−q​‖x​h‖L1\|xh_{q}\|_{L^{1}}=2^{-q}\|xh\|_{L^{1}}.

Combined with the trivial fact

Δj​∑qIq=∑|j−q|≤4Iq\Delta_{j}\sum_{q}\mbox{I}_{q}=\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}\mbox{I}_{q}

this yields

‖I‖Bp,r0\displaystyle\|\mbox{I}\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim (∑q≥−1‖Iq‖Lpr)1r\displaystyle\Big(\sum_{q\geq-1}\|\mbox{I}_{q}\|_{L^{p}}^{r}\Big)^{\frac{1}{r}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,r0.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,r}^{0}}.

Let us move to the second term II. As before one writes

IIq(x)=hq⋆(Δqv⋅∇Sq−1θ)−Δqv⋅(hq⋆∇Sq−1θ),\mbox{II}_{q}(x)=h_{q}\star(\Delta_{q}v\cdot\nabla S_{q-1}\theta)-\Delta_{q}v\cdot(h_{q}\star\nabla S_{q-1}\theta),

and then we obtain the estimate

‖IIq‖Lp\displaystyle\|\mbox{II}_{q}\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−q∥Δq∇v∥Lp∥Sq−1∇θ∥L∞\displaystyle 2^{-q}\|\Delta_{q}\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|S_{q-1}\nabla\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​∑j≤q−22j−q​‖Δj​θ‖L∞.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\sum_{j\leq q-2}2^{j-q}\|\Delta_{j}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Combined with convolution inequalities this yields

‖II‖Bp,r0≲‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,r0.\|\mbox{II}\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,r}^{0}}.

Let us now deal with the third term III. Using that the divergence of Δq​v\Delta_{q}v vanishes, we rewrite III as

III =\displaystyle= ∑q≥2ℛdiv(ΔqvΔ~qθ)−∑q≥2div(ΔqvℛΔ~qθ)+∑q≤1[ℛ,Δqv⋅∇]Δ~qθ\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq 2}\mathcal{R}\textnormal{div}(\Delta_{q}v\,\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta)-\sum_{q\geq 2}\textnormal{div}(\Delta_{q}v\,\mathcal{R}\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta)+\sum_{q\leq 1}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v\cdot\nabla]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta
=\displaystyle= J1+J2+J3.\displaystyle J_{1}+J_{2}+J_{3}.

Using Proposition 3.1-(2), we get

‖Δj​ℛ​div​(Δq​v​Δ~q​θ)‖Lp≲2j​‖Δq​v‖Lp​‖Δ~q​θ‖L∞.\displaystyle\big\|\Delta_{j}\mathcal{R}\textnormal{div}(\Delta_{q}v\,\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta)\big\|_{L^{p}}\lesssim 2^{j}\|\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{p}}\|\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Also, since Δ~q​θ\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta is supported away from zero for q≥2q\geq 2 then Proposition 3.1 (3) yields

‖Δj​div​(Δq​v​ℛ​Δ~q​θ)‖Lp\displaystyle\big\|\Delta_{j}\textnormal{div}(\Delta_{q}v\,\mathcal{R}\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta)\big\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2j​‖Δq​v‖Lp​‖ℛ​Δ~q​θ‖L∞\displaystyle 2^{j}\|\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{p}}\|\mathcal{R}\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2j​‖Δq​v‖Lp​‖Δ~q​θ‖L∞.\displaystyle 2^{j}\|\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{p}}\|\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Therefore we get

‖Δj​(J1+J2)‖Lp\displaystyle\|\Delta_{j}(J_{1}+J_{2})\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑q∈ℕq≥j−42j​‖Δq​v‖Lp​‖Δ~q​θ‖L∞\displaystyle\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}\atop q\geq j-4}2^{j}\|\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{p}}\|\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​∑q∈ℕq≥j−42j−q​‖Δq​θ‖L∞,\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}\atop q\geq j-4}2^{j-q}\|{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}},

where we have again used Bernstein inequality to get the last line. It suffices now to use convolution inequalities to get

‖J1+J2‖Bp,r0≲‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,r0.\|J_{1}+J_{2}\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,r}^{0}}.

For the last term J3J_{3} we can write

∑−1≤q≤1[ℛ,Δqv⋅∇]Δ~qθ(x)=∑q≤1[div χ~(D)ℛ,Δqv]Δ~qθ(x),\sum_{-1\leq q\leq 1}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v\cdot\nabla]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta(x)=\sum_{q\leq 1}[\textnormal{div }\widetilde{\chi}(\textnormal{D})\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta(x),

where χ~\widetilde{\chi} belongs to 𝒟⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Proposition 3.1 ensures that div ​χ~​(D)​ℛ\textnormal{div }\widetilde{\chi}(\textnormal{D})\mathcal{R} is a convolution operator with a kernel h~\tilde{h} satisfying

|h~​(x)|≲(1+|x|)−d−1.|\tilde{h}(x)|\lesssim(1+|x|)^{-d-1}.

Thus

J3=∑q≤1h~⋆(Δq​v⋅Δ~q​θ)−Δq​v⋅(h~⋆Δ~q​θ).J_{3}=\sum_{q\leq 1}\tilde{h}\star(\Delta_{q}v\cdot\tilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta)-\Delta_{q}v\cdot(\tilde{h}\star\tilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta).

First of all we point out that Δj​J3=0\Delta_{j}J_{3}=0 for j≥6j\geq 6, thus we just need to estimate the low frequencies of J3J_{3}. Noticing that x​h~x\tilde{h} belongs to Lp′L^{p^{\prime}} for p′>1p^{\prime}>1 then using Lemma 3.2 with m=p≥2m=p\geq 2 we obtain

‖Δj​J3‖L∞\displaystyle\|\Delta_{j}J_{3}\|_{L^{\infty}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑q≤1∥xh~∥Lp′∥Δq∇v∥Lp∥Δ~qθ∥Lp\displaystyle\sum_{q\leq 1}\|x\tilde{h}\|_{L^{p^{\prime}}}\|\Delta_{q}\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{p}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​∑−1≤q≤1‖Δq​θ‖Lp.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\sum_{-1\leq q\leq 1}\|{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{p}}.

This yields finally

‖J3‖Bp,r0≲‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖Lp.\|J_{3}\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{L^{p}}.

This completes the proof of the first part of Theorem 3.3. The second part can be done in the same way so that we will only give here a shorten proof. To estimate the terms I{\rm I} and II{\rm II} we use two facts: the first one is ∥Δq∇u∥L∞≈∥Δqω∥L∞\|\Delta_{q}\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}\approx\|\Delta_{q}\omega\|_{L^{\infty}} for all q∈ℕ.q\in\mathbb{N}. ∥∇Sq−1v∥L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla S_{q-1}v\|_{L^{\infty}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∥∇Δ−1v∥L∞+∑j=0q−2∥Δj∇v∥L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla\Delta_{-1}v\|_{L^{\infty}}+\sum_{j=0}^{q-2}\|\Delta_{j}\nabla v\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖ω‖Lρ+q​‖ω‖L∞.\displaystyle\|\omega\|_{L^{\rho}}+q\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}.

‖Δj​J3‖Lp\displaystyle\|\Delta_{j}J_{3}\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑q≤1∥xh~∥Lρ′∥Δq∇v∥L∞∥Δ~qθ∥Lρ\displaystyle\sum_{q\leq 1}\|x\tilde{h}\|_{L^{\rho^{\prime}}}\|\Delta_{q}\nabla v\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\rho}}

≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖ω‖Lρ​‖θ‖Lρ.\displaystyle\|\omega\|_{L^{\rho}}\|\theta\|_{L^{\rho}}.

4. Transport-Diffusion equation

In this section we will give some useful estimates for any smooth solution of a linear transport-diffusion model given by

(TD) {∂tθ+v⋅∇θ+|D|​θ=fθ|t=0=θ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta+|\textnormal{D}|\theta=f\\ \theta_{|t=0}=\theta^{0}.\end{array}\right.

We will discuss three kinds of estimates: LpL^{p} estimates, smoothing effects and logarithmic estimates.

The proof of the following LpL^{p} estimates can be found in [13].

Proposition 4.1.

Let vv be a smooth divergence-free vector field of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and θ\theta be a smooth solution of (TD)({\textnormal{TD}}). Then we have for every p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty]

‖θ⁡(t)‖Lp≤‖θ0‖Lp+∫0t‖f⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ.\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|f(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau.

We intend to prove the following smoothing effect.

Theorem 4.2.

Let vv be a smooth divergence-free vector field of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with vorticity ω\omega. Then, for every p∈[1,∞[p\in[1,\infty[ there exists a constant CC such that

supq∈ℕ2q​‖Δq​θ‖Lt1​Lp≤C​‖θ0‖Lp+C​‖θ0‖L∞​‖ω‖Lt1​Lp,\sup_{q\in\mathbb{N}}2^{q}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}}\leq C\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+C\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\omega\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}},

for every smooth solution θ\theta of (TD){\rm(TD)} with f≡0f\equiv 0.

Proof.

We start with localizing in frequencies the equation: for q≥−1q\geq-1 we set θq:=Δq​θ.\theta_{q}:=\Delta_{q}\theta. Then

∂tθq+v⋅∇θq+|D|θq=−[Δq,v⋅∇]θ.\partial_{t}\theta_{q}+v\cdot\nabla\theta_{q}+|\textnormal{D}|\theta_{q}=-[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]\theta.

Recall that θq{\theta}_{q} is real function since the functions involved in the dyadic partition of the unity are radial. Then multiplying the above equation by |θq|p−2​θq,|\theta_{q}|^{p-2}{\theta}_{q}, integrating by parts and using Hölder inequalities we get

1pdd​t∥θq∥Lpp+∫ℝ2(|D|θq)|θq|p−2θqdx≤∥θq∥Lpp−1∥[Δq,v⋅∇]θ∥Lp.\frac{1}{p}\frac{d}{dt}\|\theta_{q}\|_{L^{p}}^{p}+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(|\textnormal{D}|\theta_{q})|\theta_{q}|^{p-2}{\theta}_{q}dx\leq\|\theta_{q}\|_{L^{p}}^{p-1}\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\|_{L^{p}}.

Recall from [9] the following generalized Bernstein inequality

c​2q​‖θq‖Lpp≤∫ℝ2(|D|​θq)​|θq|p−2​θq​𝑑x,c2^{q}\|\theta_{q}\|_{L^{p}}^{p}\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(|\textnormal{D}|\theta_{q})|\theta_{q}|^{p-2}{\theta}_{q}dx,

where cc depends on pp. Inserting this estimate in the previous one we obtain

1pdd​t∥θq∥Lpp+c2q∥θq∥Lpp≲∥θq∥Lpp−1∥[Δq,v⋅∇]θ∥Lp.\frac{1}{p}\frac{d}{dt}\|\theta_{q}\|_{L^{p}}^{p}+c2^{q}\|\theta_{q}\|_{L^{p}}^{p}\lesssim\|\theta_{q}\|_{L^{p}}^{p-1}\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\|_{L^{p}}.

Thus we find

(4.1) dd​t∥θq∥Lp+c2q∥θq∥Lp≲∥[Δq,v⋅∇]θ∥Lp.\frac{d}{dt}\|\theta_{q}\|_{L^{p}}+c2^{q}\|\theta_{q}\|_{L^{p}}\lesssim\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\|_{L^{p}}.

To estimate the right hand-side, we shall use the following lemma (see the appendix for the proof of this lemma).

Lemma 4.3.

Let vv be a smooth divergence-free vector field and θ\theta be a smooth scalar function. Then, for all p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty] and q≥−1,q\geq-1,

∥[Δq,v⋅∇]θ∥Lp≲∥∇v∥Lp∥θ∥B∞,∞0.\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\|_{L^{p}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

Combined with (4.1) this lemma yields

dd​t​(ec​t​2q​‖θq​(t)‖Lp)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\big(e^{ct2^{q}}\|\theta_{q}(t)\|_{L^{p}}\big) ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ec​t​2q​‖∇v​(t)‖Lp​‖θ⁡(t)‖B∞,∞0\displaystyle e^{ct2^{q}}\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta(t)\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ec​t​2q​‖ω⁡(t)‖Lp​‖θ0‖L∞.\displaystyle e^{ct2^{q}}\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}.

To get the last line, we have used the conservation of the L∞L^{\infty} norm of θ\theta and the classical fact

∥∇v∥Lp≲∥ω∥Lp∀p∈]1,+∞[.\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\lesssim\|\omega\|_{L^{p}}\qquad\forall p\!\in]1,+\infty[.

Integrating the differential inequality we get

‖θq​(t)‖Lp\displaystyle\|\theta_{q}(t)\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖θq0‖Lp​e−c​t​2q+|θ0|∫0tL∞⁡e−c⁡(t−τ)​2q​‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\|\theta_{q}^{0}\|_{L^{p}}e^{-ct2^{q}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-c(t-\tau)2^{q}}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau.

Integrating in time yields finally

2q​‖θq‖Lt1​Lp\displaystyle 2^{q}\|\theta_{q}\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖θq0‖Lp+|θ0|∫0tL∞⁡‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ\displaystyle\|\theta_{q}^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖θ0‖Lp+|θ0|∫0tL∞⁡‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ,\displaystyle\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau,

which is the desired result. ∎

Let us now move to the last part of this section which deals with some logarithmic estimates generalizing the results of [26, 16]. First we recall the following result of propagation of Besov regularities.

Proposition 4.4.

Let (p,r)∈[1,∞]2,s∈]−1,1[(p,r)\in[1,\infty]^{2},s\in]-1,1[ and θ\theta a smooth solution of (TD). Then we have

‖θ‖L~t∞​Bp,rs≲eC​V​(t)​(‖θ0‖Bp,rs+∫0te−C​V​(τ)​‖f⁡(τ)‖Bp,rs​𝑑τ),\|\theta\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{p,r}^{s}}\lesssim e^{CV(t)}\Big(\|\theta^{0}\|_{B_{p,r}^{s}}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{-CV(\tau)}\|f(\tau)\|_{B_{p,r}^{s}}d\tau\Big),

where V⁡(t)=‖∇v‖Lt1​L∞.V(t)=\|\nabla v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}.

The proof of this result is omitted here and it can be done similarly to the inviscid case [8], using especially Proposition 4.1.

Now we will show that for the index regularity s=0s=0 we can obtain a better estimate with a linear growth on Lipschitz norm of the velocity.

Theorem 4.5.

There exists C>0C>0 such that if κ≥0\kappa\geq 0, p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty] and θ\theta a solution of

(∂t+v⋅∇+κ|D|)θ=f,(\partial_{t}+v\cdot\nabla+\kappa|\textnormal{D}|)\theta=f,

then we have

‖θ‖L~t∞​Bp,10≤C⁡(‖θ0‖Bp,10+‖f‖Lt1​Bp,10)​(1+∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ).\|\theta\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{p,1}^{0}}\leq C\Big(\|\theta^{0}\|_{B_{p,1}^{0}}+\|f\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{p,1}^{0}}\Big)\Big(1+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau\Big).
Proof.

We mention that the result is first proved in [26] for the case κ=0\kappa=0 by using the special structure of the transport equation. In [17] the first two authors generalized Vishik’s result for a transport-diffusion equation where the dissipation term has the form −κ​Δ​θ-\kappa\Delta\theta. The method described in [17] can be easily adapted here for our model.

Let q∈ℕ∪{−1}q\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{-1\} and denote by θ¯q\overline{\theta}_{q} the unique global solution of the initial value problem

(4.2) {∂tθ¯q+v⋅∇θ¯q+|D|​θ¯q=Δq​f,θ¯q|t=0=Δqθ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\overline{\theta}_{q}+v\cdot\nabla\overline{\theta}_{q}+|\textnormal{D}|\overline{\theta}_{q}=\Delta_{q}f,\\ {\overline{\theta}_{q}}_{|t=0}=\Delta_{q}\theta^{0}.\\ \end{array}\right.

Using Proposition 4.4 with s=±12s=\pm\frac{1}{2} we get

‖θ¯q‖L~t∞​Bp,∞±12≲(‖Δq​θ0‖Bp,∞±12+‖Δq​f‖Lt1​Bp,∞±12)​eC​V​(t),\|\overline{\theta}_{q}\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{p,\infty}^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}}\lesssim\big(\|\Delta_{q}\theta^{0}\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}}+\|\Delta_{q}f\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{p,\infty}^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}}\big)e^{CV(t)},

where V⁡(t)=‖∇v‖Lt1​L∞.V(t)=\|\nabla v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}. Combined with the definition of Besov spaces this yields for j,q≥−1j,q\geq-1

(4.3) ‖Δj​θ¯q‖Lt∞​Lp≲2−12​|j−q|​(‖Δq​θ0‖Lp+‖Δq​f‖Lt1​Lp)​eC​V​(t).\|\Delta_{j}\overline{\theta}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\lesssim 2^{-\frac{1}{2}|j-q|}\big(\|\Delta_{q}\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|\Delta_{q}f\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}}\big)e^{CV(t)}.

By linearity and again the definition of Besov spaces we have

(4.4) ‖θ‖L~t∞​Bp,10≤∑|j−q|≥N‖Δj​θ¯q‖Lt∞​Lp+∑|j−q|<N‖Δj​θ¯q‖Lt∞​Lp,\displaystyle\|\theta\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{p,1}^{0}}\leq\sum_{|j-q|\geq N}\|\Delta_{j}\overline{\theta}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}+\sum_{|j-q|<N}\|\Delta_{j}\overline{\theta}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}},

where N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} is to be chosen later. To deal with the first sum we use (4.3)

∑|j−q|≥N‖Δj​θ¯q‖Lt∞​Lp\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\geq N}\|\Delta_{j}\overline{\theta}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−N/2∑q≥−1(∥Δqθ0∥Lp+∥Δqf∥Lt1​Lp)eC​V​(t)\displaystyle 2^{-N/2}\sum_{q\geq-1}\big(\|\Delta_{q}\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|\Delta_{q}f\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}}\big)e^{CV(t)}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−N/2(∥θ0∥Bp,10+∥f∥Lt1​Bp,10)eC​V​(t).\displaystyle 2^{-N/2}\big(\|\theta^{0}\|_{B_{p,1}^{0}}+\|f\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{p,1}^{0}}\big)e^{CV(t)}.

We now turn to the second sum in the right-hand side of (4.4).

It is clear that

∑|j−q|<N‖Δj​θ¯q‖Lt∞​Lp≲∑|j−q|<N‖θ¯q‖Lt∞​Lp.\sum_{|j-q|<N}\|\Delta_{j}\overline{\theta}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\lesssim\sum_{|j-q|<N}\|\overline{\theta}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}.

Applying Proposition 4.1 to the system (4.2) yields

‖θ¯q‖Lt∞​Lp≤‖Δq​θ0‖Lp+‖Δq​f‖Lt1​Lp.\|\overline{\theta}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\leq\|\Delta_{q}\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|\Delta_{q}f\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}}.

It follows that

∑|j−q|<N‖Δj​θ¯q‖Lt∞​Lp≲N⁡(‖θ0‖Bp,10+‖f‖Lt1​Bp,10).\sum_{|j-q|<N}\|\Delta_{j}\overline{\theta}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\lesssim N\big(\|\theta^{0}\|_{B_{p,1}^{0}}+\|f\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{p,1}^{0}}\big).

The outcome is the following

∥θ∥L~t∞​Bp,10≲(∥θ0∥Bp,10+∥f∥Lt1​Bp,10)(2−N/2eC​V​(t)+N).\|\theta\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{p,1}^{0}}\lesssim\big(\|\theta^{0}\|_{B_{p,1}^{0}}+\|f\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{p,1}^{0}}\big)\Big(2^{-N/2}e^{CV(t)}+N\Big).

Choosing

N=[2​C​V​(t)log⁡2]+1,N=\Big[\frac{2CV(t)}{\log 2}\Big]+1,

we get the desired result.

∎

5. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Throughout this section we use the notation Φk\Phi_{k} to denote any function of the form

OPENΦk​(t)=C0​exp⁡(…​expCLOSE⏟k​t​i​m​e​s​(C0​t)​…),\Phi_{k}(t)=C_{0}\underbrace{\exp(...\exp}_{k\,times}(C_{0}t)...),

where C0C_{0} depends on the involved norms of the initial data and its value may vary from line to line up to some absolute constants. We will make an intensive use (without mentionning it) of the following trivial facts

∫0tΦk​(τ)​𝑑τ≤Φk​(t)andexp⁡(∫0tΦk​(τ)​𝑑τ)≤Φk+1​(t).\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{k}(\tau)d\tau\leq\Phi_{k}(t)\qquad{\rm and}\qquad\exp({\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{k}(\tau)d\tau})\leq\Phi_{k+1}(t).

The proof of Theorem 1.1 will be done in several steps. The first one deals with some a priori estimates for the equations (1.2). In the second one we prove the uniqueness part. Finally, we will discuss the construction of the solutions at the end of this section.

5.1. a priori estimates

As we will see the important quantities to bound for all times are ‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}} and ‖∇v​(t)‖L∞\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}. It seems that for subcritical regularities like for example Hs,s>2H^{s},s>2 or more generally Bp,rs,s>1+2pB_{p,r}^{s},\,s>1+\frac{2}{p} we need only to bound the quantity ‖∂1θ‖Lt1​L∞\|\partial_{1}\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}, which in turn controls ‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞,\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}, due to Brezis-Galloüet logarithmic estimate, see for example [23]. Even though these quantities seem to be less regular than ‖∇v‖Lt1​L∞\|\nabla v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}, it is not at all clear how to estimate them without involving the latter quantity.

When we deal with critical regularities which is our subject here one needs to bound the Lipschitz norm of the velocity and this will require some refinement analysis, especially Theorem 4.5 seems to be very crucial. To obtain a Lipschitz bound we will proceed in several steps: one of the main step is to give an L∞L^{\infty}-bound of the vorticity but due to some technical difficulties related to Riesz transforms this will be not done in a straight way. We prove before an LpL^{p} estimate with 2<p<∞2<p<\infty and this allows us to bound the vorticity in L∞L^{\infty}.

We start with recalling the LpL^{p} estimate for the temperature function. It is a direct consequence of Proposition 4.1.

Proposition 5.1.

Let (v,θ)(v,\theta) be a smooth solution of (1.2), then for all p∈[1,+∞]p\in[1,+\infty]

‖θ⁡(t)‖Lp≤‖θ0‖Lp.\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}.

We intend now to bound the LpL^{p}-norm of the vorticity and to describe a smoothing effect for the temperature.

Proposition 5.2.

If ω0∈Lp\omega^{0}\in L^{p} and θ0∈Lp∩L∞\theta^{0}\in L^{p}\cap L^{\infty} with p∈]2,∞[,p\in]2,\infty[, then

‖ω⁡(t)‖Lp+‖θ‖L~t1​Bp,∞1≤Φ1​(t).\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{p}}+\|\theta\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}B_{p,\infty}^{1}}\leq\Phi_{1}(t).
Proof.

Applying Riesz transform ℛ\mathcal{R} to the temperature equation we get

(5.1) ∂tℛθ+v⋅∇ℛθ+|D|ℛθ=−[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ.\partial_{t}\mathcal{R}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\mathcal{R}\theta+|\textnormal{D}|\mathcal{R}\theta=-[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta.

Since |D|ℛ=∂1|\textnormal{D}|\mathcal{R}=\partial_{1} then the function Γ:=ω+ℛ​θ\Gamma:=\omega+\mathcal{R}\theta satisfies

(5.2) ∂tΓ+v⋅∇Γ=−[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ.\partial_{t}\Gamma+v\cdot\nabla\Gamma=-[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta.

According to the first part of Theorem 3.3 applied with r=2r=2 we have

∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ∥Bp,20≲∥∇v∥Lp(∥θ∥B∞,20+∥θ∥Lp).\big\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\big\|_{B_{p,2}^{0}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\big(\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{0}}+\|\theta\|_{L^{p}}\big).

Using the classical embedding Bp,20↪LpB_{p,2}^{0}\hookrightarrow L^{p} which is true only for p∈[2,∞)p\in[2,\infty)

∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ∥Lp≤∥∇v∥Lp(∥θ∥B∞,20+∥θ∥Lp).\big\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\big\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\big(\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{0}}+\|\theta\|_{L^{p}}\big).

Since div​v=0{\rm div}\,v=0 then we get from the transport equation (5.2)

∥Γ(t)∥Lp≤∥Γ0∥Lp+∫0t∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ(τ)∥Lpdτ.\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\Gamma^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau.

Putting together the last two estimates we get

‖Γ⁡(t)‖Lp\displaystyle\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖Γ0‖Lp+∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖Lp​(‖θ⁡(τ)‖B∞,20+‖θ‖Lp)​𝑑τ\displaystyle\|\Gamma^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}\big(\|\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{0}}+\|\theta\|_{L^{p}}\big)d\tau
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖ω0‖Lp+‖θ0‖Lp+∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​(‖θ⁡(τ)‖B∞,20+‖θ0‖Lp)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\|\omega^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}\big(\|\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{0}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}\big)d\tau.

We have used here the Calderón-Zygmund estimates: for p∈(1,∞)p\in(1,\infty)

‖∇v‖Lp≤C​‖ω‖Lpand‖ℛ​θ0‖Lp≤C​‖θ0‖Lp.\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\leq C\|\omega\|_{L^{p}}\quad\hbox{and}\quad\|\mathcal{R}\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}\leq C\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}.

On the other hand, from the continuity of the Riesz transform and Proposition 5.1

‖ω⁡(t)‖Lp\displaystyle\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{p}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖Γ⁡(t)‖Lp+‖ℛ​θ‖Lp\displaystyle\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{p}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta\|_{L^{p}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖Γ⁡(t)‖Lp+‖θ0‖Lp.\displaystyle\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{p}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}.

This leads to

‖ω⁡(t)‖Lp≲‖ω0‖Lp+‖θ0‖Lp+∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​(‖θ⁡(τ)‖B∞,20+‖θ0‖Lp)​𝑑τ.\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{p}}\lesssim\|\omega^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}\big(\|\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{0}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}\big)d\tau.

According to Gronwall lemma we get

(5.3) ‖ω⁡(t)‖Lp≤C0​eC0​t​eC​‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,20.\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq C_{0}e^{C_{0}t}e^{C\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,2}^{0}}}.

Let N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, then we have by Bernstein inequalities and Proposition 5.2

‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,20\displaystyle\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,2}^{0}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖SN​θ‖Lt1​B∞,20+‖(Id−SN)​θ‖Lt1​B∞,10\displaystyle\|S_{N}\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,2}^{0}}+\|(\hbox{Id}-S_{N})\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{0}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim t​‖θ0‖L∞​N+∑q≥N‖Δq​θ‖Lt1​L∞\displaystyle t\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\sqrt{N}+\sum_{q\geq N}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim N​‖θ0‖L∞​t+∑q≥N2q​2p​‖Δq​θ‖Lt1​Lp.\displaystyle\sqrt{N}\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}t+\sum_{q\geq N}2^{q\frac{2}{p}}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}}.

Using Theorem 4.2 and p>2p>2 we obtain

∑q≥N−12q​2p​‖Δq​θ‖Lt1​Lp\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq N-1}2^{q\frac{2}{p}}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑q≥N−12q⁡(2p−1)​(‖θ0‖Lp+‖θ0‖L∞​∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ)\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq N-1}2^{q(\frac{2}{p}-1)}\Big(\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau\Big)
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖θ0‖Lp+2N⁡(−1+2p)|θ0|∫0tL∞⁡‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+2^{N(-1+\frac{2}{p})}\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau.

Thus, we get

‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,20≲N​‖θ0‖L∞​t+‖θ0‖Lp+2N⁡(−1+2p)|θ0|∫0tL∞⁡‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,2}^{0}}\lesssim\sqrt{N}\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}t+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+2^{N(-1+\frac{2}{p})}\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau.

We choose NN as follows

N=[log⁡(e+∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ)(1−2/p)​log⁡2]+1.{N=\Bigg[\frac{\log\Big(e+\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau\Big)}{(1-2/p)\log 2}\Bigg]+1.}

Then it follows

‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,20≲‖θ0‖L∞∩Lp+‖θ0‖L∞​t​log12⁡(e+∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ).\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,2}^{0}}\lesssim\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}\cap L^{p}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}t\log^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big(e+\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau\Big).

Combining this estimate with (5.3) we get

‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,20\displaystyle\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,2}^{0}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖θ0‖L∞∩Lp+‖θ0‖L∞​t​log12⁡(e+C0​eC0​t​eC​‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,20)\displaystyle\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}\cap L^{p}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}t\,\log^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big(e+C_{0}e^{C_{0}t}e^{C\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,2}^{0}}}\Big)
≤\displaystyle\leq C0​(1+t2)+C​‖θ0‖L∞​t​‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,2012.\displaystyle C_{0}(1+t^{2})+C\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}t\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,2}^{0}}^{\frac{1}{2}}.

Thus we get for every t∈ℝ+t\in\mathbb{R}+

‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,20≤C0​(1+t2).\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,2}^{0}}\leq C_{0}(1+t^{2}).

It follows from (5.3)

(5.4) ‖ω⁡(t)‖Lp≤Φ1​(t).\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\Phi_{1}(t).

Applying Theorem 4.2 and (5.4) we get

(5.5) 2q​‖Δq​θ‖Lt1​Lp≤Φ1​(t),∀q∈ℕ2^{q}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}}\leq\Phi_{1}(t),\qquad\forall q\in\mathbb{N}

and thus

‖θ‖L~t1​Bp,∞1≤Φ1​(t).\|\theta\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}B^{1}_{{p,\infty}}}\leq\Phi_{1}(t).

This ends the proof of Proposition 5.2.

Remark 5.3.

It is not hard to see that from (5.5) one can obtain that for every s<1s<1

(5.6) ‖θ‖Lt1​Bp,1s≤‖θ‖L~t1​Bp,∞1≤Φ1​(t).\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{p,1}^{s}}\leq\|\theta\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}B_{p,\infty}^{1}}\leq\Phi_{1}(t).

Combined with Bernstein inequalities and the fact that p>2p>2 this yields

(5.7) ‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,1ϵ≤Φ1​(t),\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{\epsilon}}\leq\Phi_{1}(t),

for every ϵ<1−2p\epsilon<1-\frac{2}{p}.

∎

We aim now at giving an L∞L^{\infty}-bound of the vorticity.

Proposition 5.4.

Let (v,θ)(v,\theta) be a smooth solution of (1.2) such that ω0,θ0∈Lp∩L∞\omega^{0},\theta^{0}\in L^{p}\cap L^{\infty} and ℛ​θ0∈L∞\mathcal{R}\theta^{0}\in L^{\infty}, with 2<p<∞.2<p<\infty. Then we have

(5.8) ‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛ​θ​(t)‖L∞≤Φ2​(t)\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Phi_{2}(t)

and

(5.9) ‖v⁡(t)‖L∞≤Φ3​(t).\|v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Phi_{3}(t).
Proof.

∙\bullet Proof of (5.8). By using the maximum principle for the transport equation (5.2), we get

∥Γ(t)∥L∞≤∥Γ0∥L∞+∫0t∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ(τ)∥L∞dτ.\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\Gamma^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau.

Since the function ℛ​θ\mathcal{R}\theta satisfies the equation

(5.10) (∂t+v⋅∇+|D|)ℛθ=−[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ,\big(\partial_{t}+v\cdot\nabla+|\textnormal{D}|\big)\mathcal{R}\theta=-[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta,

we get by using Proposition 4.1 for p=∞p=\infty that

∥ℛθ(t)∥L∞≤∥ℛθ(t)∥L∞+∫0t∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ(τ)∥L∞dτ.\|\mathcal{R}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\mathcal{R}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau.

Combining the last two estimates yields

‖Γ⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛ​θ​(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ∥Γ0∥L∞+∥ℛθ0∥L∞+2∫0t∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ(τ)∥L∞dτ\displaystyle\|\Gamma^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+2\int_{0}^{t}\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau
≤\displaystyle\leq C0+∫0t∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ(τ)∥B∞,10dτ.\displaystyle C_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}d\tau.

It follows from the second estimate of Theorem 3.3 and Proposition 5.2

‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛ​θ​(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim C0+∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖L∞∩Lp​(‖θ⁡(τ)‖B∞,1ϵ+‖θ⁡(τ)‖Lp)​𝑑τ\displaystyle C_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}\cap L^{p}}\big(\|\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{\epsilon}}+\|\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}\big)d\tau
≲\displaystyle\lesssim C0+‖ω‖Lt∞​Lp​(‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,1ϵ+t​‖θ0‖Lp)\displaystyle C_{0}+\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\big(\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{\epsilon}}+t\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}\big)
+\displaystyle+ ∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖L∞​(‖θ⁡(τ)‖B∞,1ϵ+‖θ0‖Lp)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\big(\|\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{\epsilon}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}\big)d\tau.

Let 0<ϵ<1−2p0<\epsilon<1-\frac{2}{p} then using (5.7) we get

‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛ​θ​(t)‖L∞≲Φ1​(t)+∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖L∞​(‖θ⁡(τ)‖B∞,1ϵ+‖θ0‖Lp)​𝑑τ.\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\Phi_{1}(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\big(\|\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{\epsilon}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}\big)d\tau.

Therefore we obtain by the Gronwall lemma and a new use of (5.7) that

‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛ​θ​(t)‖L∞≤Φ2​(t).\displaystyle\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Phi_{2}(t).

∙\bullet Proof of (5.9).

Let N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} to be chosen later. Using the fact that ‖Δ˙q​v‖L∞≈2−q​‖Δ˙q​ω‖L∞\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}v\|_{L^{\infty}}\approx 2^{-q}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}, we then have

‖v⁡(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖χ⁡(2−N​|D|)​v​(t)‖L∞+∑q≥−N2−q​‖Δ˙q​ω​(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|\chi(2^{-N}|\textnormal{D}|)v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\sum_{q\geq-N}2^{-q}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖χ⁡(2−N​|D|)​v​(t)‖L∞+2N​‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞.\displaystyle\|\chi(2^{-N}|\textnormal{D}|)v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+2^{N}\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Applying the frequency localizing operator to the velocity equation we get

χ⁡(2−N​|D|)​v=χ⁡(2−N​|D|)​v0+∫0t𝒫​χ​(2−N​|D|)​θ​(τ)​𝑑τ+∫0t𝒫​χ​(2−N​|D|)​div​(v⊗v)​(τ)​𝑑τ.\chi(2^{-N}|\textnormal{D}|)v=\chi(2^{-N}|\textnormal{D}|)v_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{P}\chi(2^{-N}|\textnormal{D}|)\theta(\tau)d\tau+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{P}\chi(2^{-N}|\textnormal{D}|){\rm div}(v\otimes v)(\tau)d\tau.

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} stands for Leray projector. From Bernstein inequalities, Calderón-Zygmund estimate and the uniform boundness of χ⁡(2−N​|D|)\chi(2^{-N}|\textnormal{D}|) we get

Now we will describe the last part of the a priori estimates. Following the program exposed in the beginning, the aim is to get estimates on ∇v\nabla v.

Proposition 5.5.

Let (v,θ)(v,\theta) be a smooth solution of (1.2) and ω0,θ0∈B∞,10∩Lp\omega^{0},\theta^{0}\in B_{\infty,1}^{0}\cap L^{p} with p∈]2,∞[.p\in]2,\infty[. Then

By using the logarithmic estimates of Theorem 4.5 for the equations (5.1) and (5.10), we obtain

≲\displaystyle\lesssim Φ2​(t).\displaystyle\Phi_{2}(t).

By easy computations we get

≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖ω‖Lp+∑q∈ℕ‖Δq​ω‖L∞\displaystyle\|\omega\|_{L^{p}}+\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}\|\Delta_{q}\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim Φ1​(t)+‖ω⁡(t)‖B∞,10.\displaystyle\Phi_{1}(t)+\|\omega(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}.

‖ω⁡(t)‖B∞,10≤‖Γ⁡(t)‖B∞,10+‖ℛ​θ​(t)‖B∞,10≤Φ2​(t)​(1+∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖B∞,10​𝑑τ).\displaystyle\|\omega(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\leq\|\Gamma(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\leq\Phi_{2}(t)\Big(1+\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}d\tau\Big).

‖∇v​(t)‖L∞≤Φ3​(t).\displaystyle\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Phi_{3}(t).

Let us move to the estimate of vv in the space B∞,11B_{\infty,1}^{1}. By definition we have

‖v⁡(t)‖B∞,11≲‖v⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ω⁡(t)‖B∞,10.\|v(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1}}\lesssim\|v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\omega(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}.

‖θ⁡(t)‖B∞,10\displaystyle\|\theta(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖θ0‖B∞,10​(1+∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ)\displaystyle\|\theta^{0}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\Big(1+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau\Big)

Remark 5.6.

Notice that the a priori estimates above imply that ∇θ∈Lloc1​(ℝ+,L∞)\nabla\theta\in L^{1}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\infty}). Indeed, we can establish the following estimate by combining the smoothing effect of the temperature equation with the logarithmic estimate described by Proposition 4.5,

‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,11≤C​‖θ0‖B∞,10​(1+‖∇v‖Lt1​L∞2).\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{1}}\leq C\|\theta^{0}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}(1+\|\nabla v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}^{2}).

Although we expect to use this estimate for the uniqueness part, it seems that this is not sufficient for our purpose and some technical problems arise due to the fact that Riesz transforms do not map continuously L∞L^{\infty} to itself. The crucial information that we need for the uniqueness is θ∈L~loc1​(ℝ+,Bp,∞1).\theta\in\widetilde{L}_{\textnormal{loc}}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};{B}_{p,\infty}^{1}).

We consider the following system

(Bn) {∂tvn+vn⋅∇vn+∇pn=θn​e2∂tθn+vn⋅∇θn+|D|​θn=0div​vn=0vn|t=0=Snv0,θn|t=0=Snθ0\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v_{n}+v_{n}\cdot\nabla v_{n}+\nabla p_{n}=\theta_{n}e_{2}\\ \partial_{t}\theta_{n}+v_{n}\cdot\nabla\theta_{n}+|\textnormal{D}|\theta_{n}=0\\ \textnormal{div}v_{n}=0\\ {v_{n}}_{|t=0}=S_{n}v^{0},\quad{\theta_{n}}_{|t=0}=S_{n}\theta^{0}\end{array}\right.

Now from the a priori estimates the Lipschitz norm can not blow up in finite time and then the solution (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}) is globally defined. Once again from the a priori estimates we have for 2<p<∞2<p<\infty

‖vn‖LT∞​B∞,11+‖ωn‖LT∞​Lp+‖θn‖LT∞​(B∞,10∩Lp)≤Φ3​(T).\|v_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{1}}+\|\omega_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{p}}+\|\theta_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}(B_{\infty,1}^{0}\cap L^{p})}\leq\Phi_{3}(T).

Then it follows that up to an extraction the sequence (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}) is weakly convergent to (v,θ)(v,\theta) belonging to LT∞​B∞,11×LT∞​(B∞,10∩Lp),L^{\infty}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{1}\times L^{\infty}_{T}(B_{\infty,1}^{0}\cap L^{p}), with ω∈LT∞​Lp\omega\in L^{\infty}_{T}L^{p}. For (n,m)∈ℕ2(n,m)\in\mathbb{N}^{2} we set vn,m=vn−vmv_{n,m}=v_{n}-v_{m} and θn,m=θn−θm\theta_{n,m}=\theta_{n}-\theta_{m} then according to the estimate (5.19) and (5.20) we get for T=δT=\delta

‖vn,m‖LT∞​B∞,10+‖θn,m‖LT1​Bp,12p≤Φ3​(t)​(‖Sn​v0−Sm​v0‖B∞,10+‖Sn​θ0−Sm​θ0‖Lp).\|v_{n,m}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|\theta_{n,m}\|_{L^{1}_{T}B_{p,1}^{\frac{2}{p}}}\leq\Phi_{3}(t)\big(\|S_{n}v^{0}-S_{m}v^{0}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|S_{n}\theta^{0}-S_{m}\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}\big).

This shows that (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}) is a Cauchy sequence in the Banach space LT∞​B∞,10×LT1​Bp,12pL^{\infty}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{0}\times L^{1}_{T}B_{p,1}^{\frac{2}{p}} and then it converges strongly to (v,θ).(v,\theta). This allows to pass to the limit in the system (Bn)({\rm B}_{n}) and then we get that (v,θ)(v,\theta) is a solution of the Boussinesq system (1.2).

Appendix: proof of Lemma 4.3

We have from Bony’s decomposition

[Δq,v⋅∇]θ\displaystyle[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]\theta =\displaystyle= ∑|j−q|≤4[Δq,Sj−1v⋅∇]Δjθ+∑|j−q|≤4[Δq,Δjv⋅∇]Sj−1θ\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}[\Delta_{q},S_{j-1}v\cdot\nabla]\Delta_{j}\theta+\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}[\Delta_{q},\Delta_{j}v\cdot\nabla]S_{j-1}\theta
+\displaystyle+ ∑j≥q−4[Δq,Δjv⋅∇]Δ~jθ\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq q-4}[\Delta_{q},\Delta_{j}v\cdot\nabla]\widetilde{\Delta}_{j}\theta
:⁣=\displaystyle:= Iq+IIq+IIIq.\displaystyle\mbox{I}_{q}+\mbox{II}_{q}+\mbox{III}_{q}.

Observe first that

Iq=∑|j−q|≤4hq⋆(Sj−1v⋅∇Δjθ)−Sj−1v⋅(hq⋆∇Δjθ)\mbox{I}_{q}=\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}h_{q}\star(S_{j-1}v\cdot\nabla\Delta_{j}\theta)-S_{j-1}v\cdot(h_{q}\star\nabla\Delta_{j}\theta)

where h^q​(ξ)=φ⁡(2−q​ξ)\hat{h}_{q}(\xi)=\varphi({2^{-q}}\xi). Thus, Lemma 3.2 and Bernstein inequalities yield

‖Iq‖Lp\displaystyle\|\mbox{I}_{q}\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑|j−q|≤4∥xhq∥L1∥∇Sj−1v∥Lp∥∇Δjθ∥L∞\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}\|xh_{q}\|_{L^{1}}\|\nabla S_{j-1}v\|_{L^{p}}\|\nabla\Delta_{j}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖h0‖L1​∑|j−q|≤42j−q​‖Δj​θ‖L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|h_{0}\|_{L^{1}}\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}2^{j-q}\|\Delta_{j}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,∞0.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

To estimate the second term we use once again Lemma 3.2

‖IIq‖Lp\displaystyle\|\hbox{II}_{q}\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑|j−q|≤42−q∥Δj∇v∥Lp∥∇Sj−1θ∥L∞\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}2^{-q}\|\Delta_{j}\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\nabla S_{j-1}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​∑|j−q|≤4k≤j−22k−q​‖Δk​θ‖L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4\atop k\leq j-2}2^{k-q}\|\Delta_{k}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,∞0.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

Let us now move to the remainder term. We separate it into two terms: high frequencies and low frequencies.

IIIq\displaystyle\hbox{III}_{q} =\displaystyle= ∑j≥q−4j∈ℕ[Δq∂i,Δjvi]Δ~jθ+[Δq,Δ−1v⋅∇]Δ~−1θ\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq q-4\atop j\in\mathbb{N}}[\Delta_{q}\partial_{i},\Delta_{j}v^{i}]\widetilde{\Delta}_{j}\theta+[\Delta_{q},\Delta_{-1}v\cdot\nabla]\widetilde{\Delta}_{-1}\theta
:⁣=\displaystyle:= IIIq1+IIIq2.\displaystyle\hbox{III}_{q}^{1}+\hbox{III}_{q}^{2}.

For the first term we don’t need to use the structure of the commutator. We estimate separately each term of the commutator by using Bernstein inequalities.

≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,∞0.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

For the second term we use Lemma 3.2 combined with Bernstein inequalities.
